utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, I'd like to now go to page 55 of the B/C/S, page 29 in English. I'm focusing on the words of Minister Gojko Susak at the top, and he states, quotes: "Third, Mr. President, let me just finish. Can we have your agreement, provided that we will face risks if we lose? I think that it would have a psychological effect on them if we, after the first day of the operation at Benkovac and Obrovac, take the risk of throwing leaflets which could cause losses, but we have know in advance that it is something we have risked; but we would call on them in your name, whatever kind of leaflet we make, after the first day of the operation. We would point out the routes which they could use to pull out and formulate them in such a manner to double the confusion such as it is. But we must take a risk then and find the people to do it, and I believe that there are those who would take the risk of doing it." President Tudjman responds: "A leaflet of this sort ... general chaos, the victory of the Croatian Army supported by the international community and so forth. Serbs, you are already withdrawing, and so forth, and we are appealing to you not to withdraw, we guarantee ... this means giving them a way out, while pretending to guarantee civil rights, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rajcic, you're shaking your head no. I'll ask you if you deny that President Tudjman indicated his approval for using a leaflet for the dual purpose of telling the Serbs how to leave the area, while at the same time pretending to guarantee their civil rights.

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain why I had this body language. Mr. Russo, the interpretation of what you were saying did not correspond to the text that I'm reading in the Croatian language, but that's immaterial. I did not hear words to that effect on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let's continue on a bit in the conversation, a bit further down from where Dr. Miroslav Tudjman begins to say: "If I may say so ...": "If I may say so, it is evident that they tend to listen more to the radio and television instead of reading leaflets. It's better to use radio and television." President Tudjman then responds: "Use radio and television, but leaflets as well." And Gojko Susak adds: "Use leaflets, but drop them among them. Instilling the feeling among them that you have succeeded, that you are above them, that you are dropping leaflets, this will provoke something." Now, Mr. Rajcic, Mr. Susak here is referring provoking an exodus of the civilian population, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also -- we're working on, just for the record, the translation of this document, and that's one of the translations I believe we've challenged, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the record. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any further matters to put to the witness, other than in light of the fact that we're on this issue, I would like, at this opportunity, Mr. President, to move in the audiotape of the 31 July meeting. I believe there is no objection from the Defence. That is 65 ter 4467.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Judge, I thought the audio was in already, but we certainly have no objection. Our objection had been, and I think that with Mr. Waespi, in talking to Mr. Waespi, it had been with the transcript, as to who had been saying what at various times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I can just clear that up, Mr. President. There was a shortened clip of the conversation admitted by the Defence as D960, D960. We'd like to tender the full portion, which is 65 ter 4467, and I'd also request, Mr. President, that this be linked and admitted with P461, the transcript, and whatever issues we work out with the transcript, it will simply be together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, we don't have any objection to that, in theory. We were just trying to work from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to always listen to a tape is a cumbersome exercise. Therefore, it's important that we have, of course, a well-translated transcript so that there are no further discussions about translation. I'm afraid that as far as who is speaking at what moment, that might be something that cannot too easily be resolved. You could send the experts to find out, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There was one issue, of course, taking this transcript and this tape in conjunction with Mr. French's analysis of this tape. I believe we can talk about this, but certainly that needs to be explored when looking at this as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the expert report on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, which we did not object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and where you did not seek to cross-examine the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that is true for all parties. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, P461 at this moment is the transcript only. May I take it that you would like to have attached to the transcript the audio so that it becomes P461, audio and transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in the absence of any objections, the audio is now admitted into evidence with the transcript together, the transcript being in evidence already under P461.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I indicated, my examination is concluded. I didn't know if the Court wanted to take the opportunity to take a look at the map in Mr. Rajcic's brief-case. I didn't intend to go into that. I just wanted to remind the Chamber, if there is any interest in that, we can ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be practical that we just have a glance at it, so most important is that we know what kind of map it is, without going into every detail, and then if it would circulate around the courtroom. Then we could find out whether we would like to have a copy in evidence, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can take a quick break and take a look at it, and we can consult together and look at it, also consult with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'd like to have a brief look at your map, as you said you had in your suitcase, so you didn't bring it in vain, but before we do so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rajcic, we extensively dealt with the target of the apartment of Mr. - I shouldn't make the same mistake - Mr. Martic. Do you remember how many projectiles were fired at his apartment?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to me 13 to 16, but I'm not sure. I have to check, in my documents, the reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any recollection whether all 13 or 16 hit the apartment which served as residence of Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be specific, but repeated fire confirmed that the harassment and pressure effect had been achieved; in other words, that a sense of insecurity had been instilled in Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, you do not know to what extent any adjacent apartments were hit by any of the projectiles?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have full information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When asked about what you considered when it was decided that it would be fired at this apartment, you mentioned both the principle of distinction and the principle of proportionality. You also told us that chances to hit Mr. Martic, as a person, were rather limited. Could you explain to us how, in terms of proportionality, you considered it to be appropriate to fire with a 130-millimetre on his apartment for 13 to 16 times?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, 13 to 16 rounds, not 13 to 16 times. I'm sorry, but this is military terminology. The principle of proportionality or balance is a process whereby possible civilian casualties are balanced with the success or effect that might be achieved in order to exert pressure on Milan Martic to have him possibly sign the capitulation, because he had not accepted that option for the end of the war. When we obtained information that the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had an evacuation plan and a plan on how to take care of the civilians, and also in accordance with the International Law of War, the defenders also have a huge responsibility in terms of saving civilian lives in the combat zone, and taking into account the facts that the buildings and facilities located in that area where Mile Martic had his residence were of good quality and that the residents, in accordance with the doctrine of the former JNA and the All People's Defence and social self-protection, as it was called, would do anything to take care of the population in the area. And so the decision was made to do this in this limited way. And also in light of the limited capabilities to engage this moving target, and Mile Martic was a moving target, based on the data obtained with constant surveillance and intelligence effort concentrating on Mile Martic, we felt that we could engage or use our 130-millimetre guns to exert pressure on him and to force him to accept military defeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Had Mr. Martic lived in the same apartment for a long time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, he was a police officer in Knin, and at that time, with the purpose-built apartments that was in Yugoslavia -- that was in effect in Yugoslavia, the police built apartments for its employees quite close to the police station. Well, relatively close to the police station. And last week, when we talked about Mile Martic and his residence, that's what we said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was whether he had lived there for a long period of time, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Yes, Your Honour, I don't know how long he used that apartment before and during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- I think you explained the target which was called "hospital" on the list in your 92 ter statement, but I'm just trying to find the exact --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Twenty-two, yes, it just comes before 23. You say it's a field near the crossroads outside of the northern barracks, from which you anticipated that the ARSK may attempt to withdraw military equipment or otherwise use the area to its advantage. Now, did they attempt, through that field, to withdraw military equipment or did they in any way use that field to their advantage?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that intersection, which is close to the Slavko Rodic or Northern Camp Barracks, was an intersection where there was a lot of traffic by their logistics units and the reserve forces that were being deployed to intervene on the Dinara Mountain, and in accordance with the principles and the doctrine of the use of artillery, such intersections are planned as locations where the enemy is ambushed because it is very easy to determine the X-Y coordinates for those locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The X-Y coordinates refer to a field, not to the crossroads themselves, so my question was whether your expectation that they might use the field, whether that turned out to be a reality.

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information had come in that they had a small artillery unit, a mortar unit, which was located close to the barracks in a school. I think it was a secondary school that at the time it was used for that purpose, and that empty area in front of the school was a possible firing position, which would make it possible for them to fire on Mount Dinara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Finally, in one of the annexes, I think it was the diary of the 4th Guards Brigade, I found targets by an indication by their N number, for example, N-1 or N-28. It's not entirely clear what the reference N stands for.

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a comparison with the coded map, the one that we have for the 7th Guards Brigade, Ivancica, where we spoke about S-15, S-54 and so on, and in the same way the 4th Guards Brigade had its own coded map with a different name. And the circles that you wanted to have explained to you, we have to look at the map to see where it is actually located, and then we would see that this is a quadrant N, and then there is a numerical designation next to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two of the targets thus named are -- one is N-1, Cupkovici hamlet. Do you have any recollection of what happened there that one should fire on this hamlet, or what was there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I remember correctly, as I worked on the reconstruction or preparing the documents for the Prosecution, I think - well, we would have to consult the map - that the hamlet of Cupkovici is actually the western part of Knin. The course of combat, when one infantry battalions of the 4th Guards Brigade entered the area, I assume, well, they probably had an infantry engagement, and if that is the case, then if there is strong resistance, then they try to deal with it using their own artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the clock. I have one or more questions for you. Let me inquire with the Defence. Mr. Kehoe, how much more time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We need to go back into the Brioni transcript that was brought up in cross-examination our equivalent to redirect, I'd say we probably, to go through that, would need half an hour or so on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour. Then not much time will be left today for other matters. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I want to be sure that I ask for permission that I lead that examination, if that's all right with the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's no problem, Mr. Misetic. Then would it be possible, if it exists -- first of all, could we look at the map that you brought so that the parties could look at it during the break, Mr. Rajcic, if you could, with the assistance of Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when we spoke of topographical maps, in relation to the coded map Ivancica, the question was raised of what sort of map that was. Well, when the map was made using the topographical maps of the former JNA, in the lower right-hand corner it reads: "Second edition, printed in 1978." That's what I referred to when I said that the map was made some 12 to 13 years prior to it being turned into the coded map of Ivancica. Now, the markings that you see here, well, I was toying around with it, trying to make a reconstruction for my own purposes. If necessary, I can hand the map over in the form in which it is for whoever's reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd give us an opportunity to have a look at it during the break, parties would also have a look at it, and then if there is then any need -- could you give it to Madam Usher so that she can first give it briefly to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please give it to the parties for inspection. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes -- twenty-five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I might have one additional question later, but, Mr. Misetic, I'll let you go first, because I had no access to e-court from my Chamber, so that's the reason why I couldn't verify something. If you're ready, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rajcic. Just a few further follow-up questions I have for you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Earlier on today, you were shown the Main Staff directive from the 26th of June, 1995. The order from the Main Staff to hit the ARSK headquarters and command posts in Knin with artillery and rocket fire was issued more than a month before your trip to Brioni; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The order of the Main Staff to hit command posts and communications facilities in Benkovac with artillery and rocket fire was issued one month before the meeting at Brioni on the 31st; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: After the meeting at Brioni, do you recall adding any potential targets to a target list after the meeting that weren't already on a list of potential targets before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if you or anyone else in the Split Military District, after the Brioni meeting, added any civilian facilities or civilian residences to a target list after the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Russo asked you a few questions about the meeting at Brioni, and he asked you a question in which it is purported that General Gotovina said: "A large number of civilians are already evacuating Knin and heading towards Banja Luka and Belgrade. That means that if we continue this pressure probably for some time to come, there won't be so many civilians." And then Mr. Russo put it to you that "this pressure" means artillery pressure. My question to you was: On the 31st of July, was there any artillery fire on Knin coming from the HV?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the days before the 31st of July, was there any artillery fire put on Knin by the HV?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if -- I'm speaking hypothetically now. If General Gotovina said, If we continue this pressure, and in reference to the fact that civilians are already fleeing, what kind of pressure, other than artillery pressure, could Serbs in Knin have felt such that they would want to leave?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there was mention of any pressure for civilians to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. But do you agree with me that the pressure being felt in Knin was the fact that the HV had now taken dominant positions on the Dinara mountain?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Croatian Army on the Dinara and the HVO as the right neighbour, of course, the pressure existed already at the time when we had taken the dominant features of Veliki Bat and the features called "veliki" and "malicil" [phoen] or big and small target on the Dinara, of course, without the use of artillery; let me underline that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You, yourself, in your testimony throughout your several days here have mentioned the fact that you had intelligence that people were leaving Knin. What was your understanding of why people were leaving Knin if, in fact, there was no artillery fire on Knin?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, I believe it was down to the propaganda campaign carried out by the Serbs in the area, which resulted, in a way, in intimidations of their own population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall ever telling General Gotovina that the artillery in Knin can fire with great precision? And if so, do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gotovina had already had such information about the precision of artillery that was under his command. He knew that this was my sixth attack or offensive operation in a row. Did I perhaps neglect to answer a part of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, the second part -- the second sentence of your answer, you say that: "He knew that this was my sixth attack or offensive operation in a row." What do you mean by that, in terms of the ability to fire precisely in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant is that he knew that we had trained artillery troops, experienced men, that we had artillery weaponry in proper order, in working order, and that, in a way, we were even able to exceed certain standards of precision in artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, in this time-period, a discussion about the fact that the HV did not have a lot of projectiles in its arsenal because of the fact that the operations in Grahovo and Glamoc had just been completed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This sort of caution came frequently from the generals. If you'll recall, Mr. Misetic, the directive from the Main Staff, you'll observe there that the Main Staff assigned six combat sets for the artillery that was supposed to provide support. In his order, General Gotovina allocated four combat sets only because we did not have more to go around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if, after the 31st of July, the forces of the Split Military District planned to use more artillery than they had planned to use prior to the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see where this arises out of the examination I did. I didn't go into a discussion of how much artillery was used, or the amount of artillery, or lack of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is taken directly from the transcript that Mr. Russo spent half an hour on, and I can get him the page number. It is pages 21 and 22 in my version of the transcript, where there's a discussion about the need to conserve artillery, just for his reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Page 21 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have an earlier translation, so I'm not sure if it's the exact page, but I'm looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether the witness can answer the question, and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajcic, let me repeat my question to you. Do you recall if the HV or the forces of the Split Military District decided to expend more artillery or planned to expend more artillery after the 31st of July than they had planned to use prior to the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessment, in view of the ammunition in our disposal, was such after the 31st of July that we had less ammunition at our disposal than at the time when we were going through the planning stage of selecting and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the planning for Operation Storm called for more artillery than you were actually able to use in Operation Storm; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajcic, one other question that arises out of Mr. Russo's examination, and he had asked you about this in his earlier direct, which is the fact that you, on the -- you had a meeting with General Gotovina on the evening of the 5th, where he told you to go, I believe, into the area of OG Sibenik, if I'm not mistaken; is that correct ?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, he's making direct reference to my very first direct examination, clearly not the examination I've just completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this question relates directly to Mr. Russo's questioning that this operation could have been conducted without the use of artillery, and that's why I'm asking him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, that was one of your questions, isn't it, in re-examination, cross-examination, however -- whatever you call it .

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I did ask him if, in his opinion, it could have been taken with troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajcic, again let me refresh your recollection. You recall Mr. Russo this morning asking you about a meeting you had with General Gotovina on the evening of the 5th where, and you correct me if I'm wrong, he sent you to go into the area of OG Sibenik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 5th, in the early evening, that's when we discussed my deployment along the Skradin-Kistanje-Padjene axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And refresh our recollection as to why it is that General Gotovina decided to send his chief of artillery on that axis. Why did he send you there on the evening of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why was I the choice, I don't know, that's something the general can tell you, but I know that the pace of attack in that particular area was slower; and the attack had not been unfolding in accordance with the plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you bring any of the artillery pieces from OG North to the axis in OG Sibenik on the evening of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why did you bring those artillery pieces with you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was no better artillery weaponry to be found in the area that would have been up to the task. The artillery pieces deployed there were of an older date and with little ammunition, and they were far less precise than the artillery pieces I took along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it your opinion that one of the reasons that the pace of attack on that axis in OG Sibenik was inefficient, is that because there was insufficient artillery to support the ground offensive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Rajcic, to put to you the same question that Mr. Russo did: Again, is that an example of the fact that artillery played an important role in the overall support of the ground forces of the Croatian Army in Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have just one moment, please. Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had one question which -- first of all, could I inquire with the parties whether the map is needed? It seems to be a normal geographical map of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There's no need for it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo? Madam Usher, could you please return this to the witness. There's no need to have it marked for identification either, I take it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rajcic, I have one question for you, and I'm looking at P2343. If that could be -- that's the diary of the 4th Guards Brigade, and I'm looking at, in e-court, page 40 out of 48. In the original, I do not know yet which page it is, but -- it should be 46 out of 57 in the original. Mr. Rajcic, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can see 2050 to 2350. That's the time slots, the place and the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm looking at, as a matter of fact, is at 0030 hours on the 6th of August and that should then -- perhaps I've indicated the wrong page. It would be on the next page. Yes. Now we haven't got the English anymore. I see there Cupkovici hamlet as a target to be fired at by the Artillery Rocket Company, the 6th of August, half an hour past midnight or 0030 in the morning, and N-28, the village of Pribadic. Do you have any knowledge about what was there in this hamlet on that date to be fired at, or what was there in the village? And if you could tell us where it is, if you know, then of course that would be appreciated as well.

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time, 0030, I was en route from Livno to Sibenik. Now, I don't know whether this is the Artillery Rocket Group of the 4th Guards Brigade or the Artillery Group 3. I can't really decipher this. And, now, as for the position of the R-22, R-37, N-16 and N-1, N-28; and you have the actual locations in brackets, I should do a reconstruction on the map. According to an overview that we have on this map, it's the 4th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It appears in the diary of the 4th Guards Brigade, so that --

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I would like to say: I have the positions here, the times for the battalions of the 4th Guards Brigade when, in the afternoon of the 5th, the actual locations that they reached at that time. In order to find those locations, I would have to have their coded map or the extension of the left side of the segment of this map in order to be able to locate those villages, in order to be able to reconstruct. But, at any rate, I was en route from Livno to Sibenik at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no specific knowledge on what was there in Cupkovici hamlet, either in terms of combat or in terms of facilities, which was needed to be fired at, at that date and that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO RAJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my assessment will be subjective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps if you don't know, then rather refrain from speculations. I take it that those last answers have not triggered any further need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rajcic, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for spending considerable time with us, answering the questions of the parties and the questions of the Bench, and I would like to wish you a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for summoning me. I do have a request to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you address me with a request.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to ask your permission to greet the generals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Rajcic, this is uncommon to do. At the same time, they have heard that you wished to greet them, which is a kind of a greeting as well. If you would accept that as my explanation, then you are invited to follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About tomorrow, we have reserved time in the morning. But before we decide whether or not to use that time, I'd like to know how much time, Mr. Russo, the videolink witness of tomorrow afternoon would take in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Approximately half an hour to 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the Defence teams, how much time they need with the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just add to that, I think Mr. Hedaraly told me it was about 20 minutes, but be that as it may. Mr. Hedaraly just bumped into one another in the cafeteria, but be that as it may, taking half an hour to 45 minutes, I'd say, you know, 45 minutes to an hour, say an hour, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's unlikely, Your Honour, we'll have any questions for that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's the same for the Markac Defence as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that in the worst scenario we would have one hour and 45 minutes for the witness. Perhaps to be added to that, perhaps some questions in relation to protective measures. The Chamber does not know yet whether we'll have any questions in that respect or whether we'll determine the matter without putting further questions to the witness. Because there are two other matters which we'd like to deal with tomorrow, one is we have still to finish the MFI list - we did not go through it entirely when we had a housekeeping session - I have no illusion that we could deal with all the newest MFIs, already, Mr. Russo, that may take more time to consider. That's one. There is another issue that is a motion that was filed by the Markac Defence in relation to a witness which is scheduled, I think, for Thursday. The Chamber would like to have some time to further hear from -- first of all, from the Prosecution, what their answer to the motion is, because two weeks would not do very well, Mr. Russo, under the present circumstances. If the parties are confident that we could deal with this, that means on the issue of the witness for Thursday, Witness 82, if that would take not more than half an hour altogether, that's 15 minutes from each party; and I'm confident that we would not need more time than 45 minutes for an MFI session to get rid of the old MFIs. If I look at all this, we could skip tomorrow morning's reserved time and tomorrow, in the afternoon, first deal with the witness and after that with the procedural matters. But if the parties feel that they are not as confident as I did that we could do it in that time, then of course we have to start in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not certain of the extent of the Markac motion, but from the Gotovina Defence, Judge, it sounds to me that we could do this, reasonably confident that we can, with the caveat of the Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I understand you correctly, we'll be given approximately 15 minutes each to make oral submissions on the issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if you would file a written response tomorrow morning, then, of course -- then we would know -- that might even save time in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I certainly can't guarantee that at this point, Mr. President, but we'll certain make every effort to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other submissions in respect of the scheduling issue? Then I'd like to turn into private session for one minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 24th of February, 2009, at quarter past 2.00 in this same Courtroom I.
